title: Red aviation lights on wind turbines do not increase bat-turbine collisions: Bats are not attracted to aviation lighting

# **Red aviation lights on wind turbines do not increase bat–turbine collisions**

Victoria J. Bennett[1,2] * & Amanda M. Hale[2]

1 Institute for Environmental Studies, School of Geology, Energy, and the Environment, Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, TX, USA 2 Department of Biology, Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, TX, USA

## **Keywords**

attraction hypothesis; bat migration; bat–wind turbine interactions; fatality monitoring surveys; foraging resources; wind energy.

## **Correspondence**

Victoria J. Bennett, Department of Biology, Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, TX 76129, USA. Tel: +1817 257 6033; Fax: +1817 257 6177 Email: v.bennett@tcu.edu

Editor: Darren Evans Associate Editor: Michael Schaub

Received 26 July 2013; accepted 19 December 2013 doi:10.1111/acv.12102

## **Abstract**

Many hypotheses have been proposed to explain why bat–wind turbine collisions occur; however, most of these hypotheses have yet to be tested and with high numbers of bat fatalities reported annually at wind resource facilities globally, there is a real need to understand this phenomenon. In this study, we tested whether aviation lighting influenced the number of bat fatalities at wind turbines. Thus, at a utility-scale wind facility in north-central Texas, we explored whether bat fatalities were higher at wind turbines with red flashing aviation lighting compared with turbines without such lighting. Over a 5-year period, we recorded fatalities at wind turbines as part of a long-term fatality monitoring programme. During standardized searches, we collected 916 bat carcasses representing all six species known to be present at the site. We found that bat fatalities were higher at wind turbines without aviation lighting compared with those with; a pattern that was driven by one species, _Lasiurus borealis_ , and there was no significant difference between fatalities at wind turbines with or without aviation lighting for any other species. Our study demonstrates that wind turbines should continue to be fitted with synchronized, flashing red aviation lights, as this form of lighting does not appear to be one of the potential causes of bat fatalities at wind resource facilities. We therefore support further research that explores possible alternative causes of bat–wind turbine interactions. More specifically, we reiterate that there is still a pressing need to determine the aspects of bat ecology that result in individuals coming into contact with wind turbines.

## **Introduction**

The impact of artificial lights on wildlife is well documented. Studies have shown that in some cases artificial lights can have implications for wildlife (Polak _et al_ ., 2011; Dwyer _et al_ ., 2013). This effect is highly dependent on species, life history stage and activity (Longcore & Rich, 2004; Stone, Jones & Harris, 2009; Santos _et al_ ., 2010). Overall, studies have revealed that artificial lights can alter the behaviour of animals, which can, in turn, lead to changes in community structure (Kociolek _et al_ ., 2010; Davies, Bennie & Gaston, 2012; Davies _et al_ ., 2013). In the presence of artificial lighting, many bird and mammal species alter their foraging and breeding habits (Bird, Branch & Miller, 2004; Kempenaers _et al_ ., 2010; Rotics, Dayan & Kronfeld-Schor, 2011). For example, a number of bird species conduct their dawn chorus hours before dawn, and some species even continue to sing throughout the night in response to artificial lighting (Longcore & Rich, 2004; Miller, 2006). Similarly, bat species that normally emerge from roost sites at dusk have been recorded emerging hours later when their roost site entrances are illuminated (Downs _et al_ ., 2003; Scanlon &

Petit, 2008). As a result, these bats spend less time foraging, which can have negative implications on their survival and breeding success (Laidlaw & Fenton, 1971; Boldogh, Dobrosi & Samu, 2007). In a similar context, many species, including bats, are light-sensitive. As a result, areas that are illuminated by artificial lighting may be avoided by such species, essentially representing another cause of habitat loss and fragmentation (Stone _et al_ ., 2009; Stone, Jones & Harris, 2012). Furthermore, artificial lighting has been found to attract wildlife, particularly individuals that are migrating (Rich & Longcore, 2006; Kociolek _et al_ ., 2010; Miles _et al_ ., 2010). In some of these cases, artificial lights appear to disorientate wildlife, such as birds and bats, causing them to collide into nearby or associated structures (Wiese _et al_ ., 2001; McGuire & Fenton, 2010). Yet in other instances, lighting has had an indirect influence by exposing individuals to predation (Longcore & Rich, 2004). Essentially, by attracting certain individuals, artificial lighting can create high-quality foraging resources for predators. Subsequently, there are numerous studies that show that lighttolerant species have taken advantage of such resources (Santos _et al_ ., 2010). For example, invertebrates attracted to

artificial lights are an abundant food source for both birds and bats (Blake _et al_ ., 1994; Thurber & Komar, 2002; Lebbin _et al_ ., 2007; Jung & Kalko, 2010).

Nevertheless, there are concerns that foraging resources created by artificial lighting may represent an ecological trap as individuals that come into contact with structures with lights like wind turbines, communication towers, or utility posts, may experience an increased risk of mortality (e.g. Coelho _et al_ ., 2012). For example, to date, thousands of bat fatalities have been reported at wind energy facilities globally (Arnett _et al_ ., 2008; Arnett & Baerwald, 2013). Consequently, conservation practitioners and wind energy developers are trying to determine why bats are coming into contact with wind turbines and devise effective mitigation strategies to minimize fatalities. Cryan & Barclay (2009) proposed that bats could be attracted to wind turbines as a result of aviation lighting, either because they were attracted to the aviation lights, or because they were attracted to aggregations of invertebrate prey attracted to the lighting.

Thus, to test whether the presence of aviation lighting affected the number of bat fatalities at wind turbines, we compared bat fatalities at wind turbines with and without aviation lighting collected during a long-term fatality monitoring programme at a utility-scale wind facility in northcentral Texas. If aviation lights on the nacelles of wind turbines were attracting bats or were attracting invertebrate aggregations, which in turn attracted bats, we would expect there to be a higher frequency of bat fatalities at wind turbines with aviation lighting compared with those without.

## **Materials and methods**

We conducted our study at Wolf Ridge Wind, LLC, which is owned and operated by NextEra Energy Resources. The site

falls within the cross timbers and prairies ecoregion of northcentral Texas (33°43′ 53.538′′ N, 97°24′ 18.186′′ W, Fig. 1) and consists of 75 1.5-MW General Electric wind turbines extended over a 48-km[2] area. Wolf Ridge became operational in October 2008, and as a part of the TCU-NextEra Wind Research Initiative, we have conducted fatality monitoring surveys at the site from 2009 to 2013, primarily from July to October of each year. This period was considered to coincide with the migration of bat species through the area. Each wind turbine consists of an 80-m tower with three 42-m blades attached to the front of the nacelle, thus creating a rotor swept zone with an 84-m diameter extending 122 m above ground. Twenty-three of the 75 wind turbines at the facility had Federal Aviation Administration lighting, consisting of an L-864 red strobe, light-emitting diode flashing beacon with a peak intensity of 2000 candela and a rate of ∼ 30 pulses min[–1] , mounted on the nacelle hub at a height of 82.5 m (Fig. 1). The remaining 52 wind turbines had no lighting of any kind (Fig. 1). Among the wind turbines, 20 were located in cattle-grazed pastures surrounded by shrub– woodland habitat (7 with aviation lighting and 13 without); 30 were located in open cattle-grazed pastures (10 with aviation lighting and 20 without); and 25 were located near the edges of shrub–woodland habitat in open cattle-grazed pastures (6 with aviation lighting and 19 without). Furthermore, each wind turbine was searched on a 1 to 6 day search interval throughout the survey period. Vegetation height in all search plots was also kept low (via cattle grazing or mowing), which ensured that our ability to search for bat carcasses was consistent across the wind resource facility (i.e. visibility was high among all the wind turbines).

In fatality monitoring surveys, we employed a rope search method (Baerwald _et al_ ., 2009). For these surveys, a 35–65-m rope was extended from the base of a wind turbine,

along which two to three technicians were spaced 4.5 m apart from the end of the rope furthest from the wind turbine. The technicians held the rope taut, and walked slowly around the wind turbine while scanning the ground in front of them for carcasses. When a carcass was found, the technician marked the location with a survey flag, and then continued the search until the rope was completely wrapped about the turbine tower. For each carcass found, we recorded the date, species (confirmed using DNA barcoding in the lab), and the bearing and distance from the turbine. We used two-sample _t_ -tests to compare the mean number of bat carcasses found per search at wind turbines with aviation lighting and those without aviation lighting. We conducted this test for all species combined, as well as for five of the six species with > 15 bat carcasses collected. We conducted all statistical analyses using Minitab 16.2.4 (2013; Minitab Inc., State College, PA, USA).

## **Results**

Over the 5-year survey period, we found 916 bat carcasses during 13 604 standardized wind turbine searches at Wolf Ridge Wind, LLC. This included 551 eastern red bats _Lasiurus borealis_ , 258 hoary bats _Lasiurus cinereus_ , 3 silverhaired bats _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ , 22 tri-coloured bats _Perimyotis subflavus_ , 49 evening bats _Nycticeius humeralis_ , 30 Mexican free-tailed bats _Tadarida brasiliensis_ and 3 unidentified bats (i.e. DNA sample was too degraded for genetic analysis). A total of 10 555 (78%) fatality searches were conducted at wind turbines without lighting, whereas 3049 (22%) were conducted at wind turbines with aviation lighting.

Using a two-sample _t_ -test, we found a significant difference in the mean number of bat fatalities for all species per search at wind turbines with aviation lighting compared with those without ( _t_ = 2.47, degrees of freedom = 73, _P_ = 0.016, 95% confidence interval of the difference in means = 0.005–0.048; Fig. 2). When we analysed the data by species, we found no difference in mean fatality rates at turbines with and without aviation lighting for hoary bats, tri-coloured bats, evening bats and Mexican free-tailed bats

(Table 1). For eastern red bats, however, we observed significantly more fatalities at wind turbines without aviation lighting, thus we can reject the hypothesis that the presence of red aviation lighting attracts bats to wind turbines (Table 1).

## **Discussion**

Our study tested whether flashing red aviation lights on the top of wind turbine nacelles influenced the number of bat– wind turbine collisions at a utility-scale wind facility. Pooling across all bat species commonly retrieved in fatality searches at Wolf Ridge Wind, LLC, we found significantly higher fatality rates at wind turbines without lighting compared with those with lighting. However, this pattern was driven by one species, the eastern red bat. For the remaining four species of bats, we found no evidence of a relationship between bat fatality rates and the presence or absence of lighting on the turbine nacelles. The results of our study may

be explained by the type of lighting used on the wind turbines. It is commonly acknowledged that the responses of animals to artificial lights depend on wavelength (i.e. the colour of the light; Downs _et al_ ., 2003, Poot _et al_ ., 2008). Studies have shown that moths are less attracted to artificial lighting with long wavelengths, such as red lights, and thus will not be in sufficient numbers to attract bats, unlike green, blue or white lights (Blake _et al_ ., 1994; van Langevelde _et al_ ., 2011). Consequently, it is unlikely that the red aviation lighting on wind turbines is attracting invertebrate prey, thus supporting the hypothesis that bats are not interacting with wind turbines to access invertebrate prey that are themselves attracted to the aviation lighting.

Similarly, although red lights are thought to disorient and attract migratory birds (Poot _et al_ ., 2008; Gehring, Kerlinger & Manville, 2009), studies have shown that bats behave the same when red lights are present as they do in unlit conditions (e.g. Downs _et al_ ., 2003). This suggests that bats are not attracted to or disorientated by red lights, and further supports our findings that bats are not attracted to the aviation lighting on wind turbines. Furthermore, light wavelength may explain why eastern red bat fatalities were lower at wind turbines with lights than those without. Stone _et al_ . (2012) demonstrated that some bat species are more sensitive to lighting than others and the eastern red bat is sensitive to light, in the sense that it is the only species present at our study site that is known to actively use lighting (such as white, yellow and orange street lights) as a foraging resource (Ammerman, Hice & Schmidly, 2012). It is plausible that eastern reds can discern between lights with different wavelengths while other bat species do not and thus they may avoid lights that are, for example, red. This hypothesis certainly warrants further investigation as a potentially deterrent, especially as eastern red bats are one of the top three bat species commonly killed at wind energy facilities in the US (Arnett _et al_ ., 2008).

Overall, our study on bat fatality supports the recommendations made by Kerlinger _et al_ . (2010) for aviation lighting with regard to birds, that wind turbines should continue to be fitted with synchronized, flashing red aviation lights. Although our study has demonstrated that bats are not coming into contact with wind turbines as a result of aviation lighting, there are still many other factors that could potentially be attracting bats to wind turbines (e.g. Cryan & Barclay, 2009). Areas of research may include studies that further explore the attraction hypothesis proposed by Cryan & Barclay (2009), which suggests as one possibility that bats are coming into contact with wind turbines because they represent a potential resource (such as foraging, roosting or mating). For example, studies have shown that invertebrates are attracted to common wind turbine surface colours, such as white and light grey (Long, Flint & Lepper, 2011). Thus, if invertebrates are aggregating on wind turbine surfaces, this in turn could be attracting bats. Alternatively, bats could be misidentifying wind turbines as a resource (i.e. bats may perceive wind turbines to be large trees in the landscape; Cryan & Barclay, 2009). Nevertheless, it is clear that our main priority is to identify which aspects of bat ecology

result in individuals coming into contact with wind turbines. We therefore support further research that continues to explore possible causes of bat–wind turbine interactions as it will provide much needed insights into how we can alleviate bat fatalities at wind facilities globally.
